name: Colin Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel. We’re independent of employers, AI companies and government, and your answers stay confidential. Walk me through a usual workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27, an MBA graduate, and lead twelve schedulers at a large building-maintenance company. We assign technicians to repairs, approve overtime, and tell big customers why a boiler is still cold. I’m very good at finding a workable plan when a van breaks down, but a tidy roster on a screen can hide three impossible journeys.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your home situation, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share an apartment with my partner, who teaches music lessons. My pay is ordinary for a manager and we have about four months of bills saved; lesson bookings are uneven, so we watch the bank balance. There are some similar operations jobs around here. I use an AI drafting tool now and then for a bland customer update, but I check the dates myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the schedulers AI Plateau is another small aid, like a better search box for our work orders. The person who sends a technician to the wrong address still has to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our team stays much the same. Routine messages might take less time, but overtime and fuel costs were already squeezing our budget. At home, my partner’s lesson bookings can dip without warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d continue checking the morning route board with the senior scheduler. If the small AI feature arrives, I’d try it on ten old work orders and count whether it picks the correct site entrance. I’d keep our current automatic transfer into the four-month savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my job. The household budget needs watching, but no radical change means I can keep doing what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the site entrance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school might have a service gate on the opposite road from the main door. A driver loses forty minutes when we give the wrong site entrance. Last Tuesday I caught one before the van left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the feature if nine of ten were right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on live dispatch. I would ask the vendor to fix the tenth and try another batch. I have no problem with tools that prove themselves.

say: **AI Plateau** would make routine work orders a little quicker.
The team still owns **wrong addresses** and late repairs.
think: Our **staffing** looks stable in this mild scenario.
Fuel and overtime costs plus uneven **lesson bookings** still need watching.
do: **Check** the morning route board with the senior scheduler.
**Try** a small feature on ten old orders before using it live.
**Continue** the existing savings transfer each month.
feel: I feel **calm** about my job, attentive to household costs.
S0.quote: A driver loses forty minutes when we give the wrong site entrance.
fieldNote: His **four-month reserve** and stable team explain the calm mood despite ordinary budget pressure.
He accepts a tool only after **site-specific testing** and catches physical details a route board can hide.

steps.text: Check the morning technician route board with the senior scheduler
Test the AI feature on ten old work orders before live dispatch
Continue monthly transfers into the four-month household savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could write replies, book visits and plan routes faster than we do now. I would ask the team to mark every visit where the software’s route did not match the real road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Behind closed doors, our desk work is exactly what the card names. My skill with breakdowns matters, but the company could run a smaller scheduling team. I could lose hours or a role if headquarters decides the model is good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join a company pilot if it uses live technician feedback, and I’d log missed entrances and broken route assumptions. I’d take the paid dispatch-system training if my manager approves a place. When the system is rolled out, I’d ask for the senior exception desk if that vacancy exists, and we’d postpone our winter trip to keep the savings buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. I can show what the tool misses, but I cannot set the number of schedulers headquarters keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a broken assumption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One van cannot be at two buildings ten kilometres apart at nine. A route model can hide an impossible schedule by marking both jobs green. I would attach the driver’s actual clock-in times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why postpone the trip now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I paid only a deposit, and the rest is due in six weeks. We agreed to hold off until we know whether my team keeps its hours. If the pilot shows no cuts, we can reconsider.

say: **Bookings and routes** may speed up, but the team must flag real-world misses.
I’d use **driver times** to challenge a route marked complete.
think: A smaller scheduling desk could cut my **hours or post**.
My breakdown skill may not outweigh headquarters’ **headcount target**.
do: **Join** the pilot and log missed entrances with driver clock-in times.
**Take** paid dispatch training if my manager approves a place.
**Postpone** the winter trip until our team hours are clearer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller team and household income.
S1.quote: A route model can hide an impossible schedule by marking both jobs green.
fieldNote: His **pilot** pairs software results with technician evidence, reflecting a cautious but active approach.
The **trip deposit** is already paid; postponing the balance protects savings while hours remain uncertain.

steps.text: Join the pilot and compare routes with driver clock-in times
Postpone the unpaid balance of the winter trip until hours are clear
Take paid dispatch-system training if the manager approves a place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could do almost all scheduling and customer messages cheaply. We should demand a date for decisions and be honest with customers about who will answer problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work could vanish by 2028, and hands-on robots only follow around 2031. Our technicians may keep going for a while, but the twelve schedulers could be cut quickly. Four months of bills buys a pause; it does not replace a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask the operations director when staff decisions will be made and request my pay and severance figures from payroll. This year I’d apply for two open field-operations supervisor jobs if their salaries cover our rent and lesson-income swings. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk ends, I’d accept a field role only after checking it is still a real vacancy with actual site duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. I can make calls and apply, but a two-year clock is short for a team built on screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we may need to live on the four-month buffer for a while, but we should not spend it before I see a cut notice. My partner can keep teaching lessons; I would not ask them to carry all our rent. We would look at the bills together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What site duties would you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Visiting buildings, checking whether work was finished and talking with technicians and customers in person. I know robots around 2031 could change some of that later. I would still rather have an offer with those tasks than a vague promise of an AI oversight post.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs a decision date and a named contact for customers.
I’d tell schedulers the desk is **exposed**, rather than promise safety.
think: The twelve-person scheduling desk could be cut in **2028**, before site robots around 2031.
Four months saved cannot **replace wages** for long.
do: **Ask** the director tomorrow for decision dates and payroll for severance figures.
**Apply** for two open field supervisor jobs only if salaries cover household bills.
**Accept** a field role after 2028 only if duties and vacancy are real.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a short clock for my screen-based team.
S2.quote: Four months of bills buys a pause; it does not replace a wage.
fieldNote: His **four-month buffer** limits immediate harm but does not make job loss safe.
He checks **salary and site duties** before treating a field vacancy as an escape from desk automation.

steps.text: Apply for two field supervisor vacancies if salaries cover household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test where a human manager still helps during repairs. We should track callbacks and completed work, not just the number of visits booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduling screen could still be mostly automated in 2031, with capable robots reaching hands-on work around 2034. I may need to work closer to buildings. Five years is enough to try that while the company still pays me, but I cannot assume a post will open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next summer, in 2027, I’d spend two afternoons each month riding with a technician, with my manager’s approval, and note where office instructions fail. I’d take the company’s paid site-supervision course if a place opens without a salary cut. Once AGI arrives around 2031, I’d apply for a field supervisor vacancy only if travel costs leave at least my current take-home pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I have room to test the ground. A site visit will tell me more than a polished course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from the last ride-along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician carries two spare valves that never appear in our parts list. We booked a second visit that was not needed. I would use those small findings to change the dispatch notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your manager refuses more rides?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my desk job and ask for the reason. I cannot disappear from my team for half a day without cover. The course would also have to fit paid work hours.

say: **Five years** lets us test the value of human repair oversight.
I’d count **callbacks**, not only visits booked.
think: Scheduling could change in **2031**, while hands-on robots arrive around 2034.
A **field post** may suit me, but an opening is not guaranteed.
do: **Ride** with a technician twice monthly next summer in 2027 if my manager approves cover.
**Take** a paid site-supervision course only if a place opens without a pay cut.
**Apply** after 2031 for field supervision only if fares leave current take-home pay.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test real site work.
S3.quote: A site visit will tell me more than a polished course brochure.
fieldNote: His **ride-alongs** turn dispatch mistakes into concrete evidence and require manager-approved team cover.
His **course and job** plans both depend on paid places, salary and travel costs.

steps.text: Ride with a technician twice monthly in summer 2027 if the manager approves cover
Take paid site-supervision training if a place opens without a pay cut
Apply after 2031 for field work only if fares preserve take-home pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives employers a decade to stop hiding behind short training announcements. Publish which scheduling and site jobs will remain, what they pay, and what workers must learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I could pay off my student loan and build more than four months of savings if our wages stay steady. Desk scheduling may still fall to AGI in 2036; capable robots arrive around 2039 and could narrow site work too. I might manage service quality by then, but I would not bet the rent on that title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep supervising the dispatch board and increase the savings transfer after the student loan is cleared, if lesson income holds. I’d ask for a paid annual rotation through service quality and take it if offered with my salary intact. In the first year after 2036, I’d seek a quality manager role only if the job still has people and site responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long end point, but not trapped. Ten years gives my partner and me time to choose based on actual offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to increase savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already transfer something each month, and the loan payment eats the spare money. Once it ends, I would send that amount into the reserve rather than a new car. That assumes lesson income keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a quality role real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A budget, a team and authority to send a technician back when a repair fails. A dashboard title without authority over repairs would leave me watching numbers. I would ask to see the job description and pay before applying.

say: A **decade** calls for published jobs, pay and learning requirements.
I’d want quality roles with **real authority** over failed repairs.
think: Clearing the **student loan** could allow a larger reserve if wages hold.
Desk work faces AGI in **2036**, while site robots follow around 2039.
do: **Keep** supervising dispatch and the current savings transfer in 2026.
**Increase** savings after the loan ends if lesson income holds.
**Take** a paid service-quality rotation if offered without a pay cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but able to plan with my partner over a decade.
S4.quote: A dashboard title without authority over repairs would leave me watching numbers.
fieldNote: He protects **household income** by linking increased saving to loan payoff and stable music-lesson bookings.
His **quality path** requires a paid rotation and a role with actual budget and site authority.

steps.text: Keep supervising dispatch and making the existing savings transfer
Increase reserve transfers after loan payoff if lesson income holds
Take a paid service-quality rotation if offered without a pay cut
Check quality manager vacancies for budget and site authority after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My schedulers could lose their work long before robots arrive on site, and four months of savings would run down fast. A firm decision date, real severance figures and paid access to site training would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the technicians whether the route software describes the roads they actually drive. I manage the board, but they carry the cost of a bad promise to a customer. Technicians’ time belongs in the numbers.

headlineQuote: Technicians’ time belongs in the numbers.
portrait: **Colin, 27**, is an MBA-trained manager leading twelve schedulers at a large building-maintenance company.
He earns **typical pay**, has about four months saved and can see some nearby operations jobs.
He uses an **AI drafting tool** occasionally and tests new systems against drivers’ real journeys.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau, anxious under steady change and alarmed by AGI in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase the scheduling desk before four months of savings protects his household.
whatWouldHelp: A firm **decision date**, severance figures and paid site training would help him plan.
